Series::item¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signatures¶

template<class T>
T Series::item() const

Scalar Series::item() const

Crossing Into A C++ Scalar¶

item() extracts the value of a rank-zero Series. It is the deliberate boundary between array computation and ordinary C++ control flow: use it when a result must become a loop condition, log value, test assertion, configuration number, or argument to an API that accepts a native scalar rather than a Series.

The precondition is deliberately about rank, not merely element count. Shape [] is a scalar and may be extracted. Shapes [1], [1,1], and higher-rank singletons remain arrays and are rejected. Use pull() for a 1-D Series or host() for a rank-aware host representation.

The typed overload, item<T>(), converts the value to the requested C++ type. The untyped overload preserves the Series dtype in a tagged pluss::Scalar, which is useful when generic code does not know the dtype at compile time. Complex extraction must be explicit through item<pluss::Complex64>() or item<pluss::Complex128>(); the tagged scalar intentionally has no complex storage alternative.

Ownership, Platform, And Autodiff¶

The returned value owns its scalar bits and does not alias Series storage. Extracting from an accelerator-backed Series performs the required host synchronization and transfer, so repeated per-element item() calls are a poor way to inspect a device result. Transfer or aggregate once, then extract.

item() is not differentiable because its return value is no longer a Series. It does not mutate or detach the receiver, but no reverse-mode edge can continue through the native C++ value. Keep calculations in Series form until the final observation boundary.

Examples¶

1. Extract native Boolean, integer, and floating values¶

std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "bool=" << pluss::make_series(true).item<bool>() << '\n'
          << "int=" << pluss::make_series(7).item<std::int64_t>() << '\n'
          << "double=" << pluss::make_series(3.5).item<double>() << '\n';

Output¶

bool=true
int=7
double=3.5

Spell the destination type explicitly when downstream C++ code requires an exact type. Numeric conversion follows the same representability constraints as the corresponding host materialization.

2. Scalar rank, not numel(), controls the contract¶

const auto singleton = pluss::make_series({42.0});
std::cout << "dim=" << singleton.dim()
          << " values=" << singleton.pull<double>().front() << '\n';

try {
  (void)singleton.item<double>();
} catch (const std::exception& error) {
  std::cout << error.what() << '\n';
}

Output¶

dim=1 values=42
Series::item<T>(): expected a rank-zero Series

The one-element vector is intentionally not collapsed into a scalar. This keeps rank visible at the C++ boundary and prevents accidental acceptance of a mis-shaped result.

3. Preserve runtime dtype with the tagged overload¶

std::cout << pluss::make_series(7).item() << '\n'
          << pluss::make_series(2.25).item() << '\n';

Output¶

Scalar(dtype=int64, value=7)
Scalar(dtype=float64, value=2.25)

pluss::Scalar carries both the value and its ScalarType. Use this overload for dtype-generic inspection; use item<T>() when a native type is already known.

4. Extract a complex scalar explicitly¶

using Complex = std::complex<double>;

const auto z = pluss::make_series(
    std::vector<Complex>{{2.0, -3.0}}, {});
std::cout << z.item<Complex>() << '\n';

Output¶

(2,-3)

The empty shape passed to the factory creates a rank-zero complex Series. Calling the untyped item() overload on this value is rejected because the tagged scalar does not erase a complex value into a misleading real scalar.

5. Extract a final reduction, not every source lane¶

const auto values = pluss::make_series({1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5});
const double total = values.sum().item<double>();
std::cout << total << '\n';

Output¶

12

This performs one host extraction after the reduction. It is preferable to calling select(...).item<double>() four times, especially on an accelerator.

6. Reject ambiguous extraction¶

try {
  (void)pluss::make_series({1, 2}).item<std::int64_t>();
} catch (const std::exception& error) {
  std::cout << error.what() << '\n';
}

Output¶

Series::item<T>(): expected a rank-zero Series

Reduce or select explicitly before extraction. The failure protects code from silently reading only the first lane of a larger result.

See Also¶

  • dim() reports whether the receiver is rank zero.

  • pull() exports a rank-one Series as std::vector<T>.

  • host() exports any rank without collapsing its structure.

  • select() chooses one lane while remaining inside Series.

  • tensor() provides the external tensor interoperability boundary in enabled builds.
